{"id": "4d90431e-e950-402b-bd15-071d41edf22a", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_bqFy8IpbK9vWV91aCFUTm6", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Mounting EFS file systems using the EFS mount helper\",\"context\":\"# Mounting EFS file systems using the EFS mount helper\\n\\nAfter you install the Amazon EFS client (`amazon-efs-utils`), you can use\\nthe EFS mount helper to mount EFS file systems on your EC2 Linux and Mac\\ninstances running a supported distributions.\\nAmazon EFS does not support mounting from EC2 Windows instances.\\n\\n**Important:**\\n\\nWe recommend that you always use the most current version of\\n`amazon-efs-utils` to ensure successful mounting. For example, versions\\nof `amazon-efs-utils` prior to 2.3 do not support mounting with IPv6\\naddresses.\\n\\nWhen mounting a file system, the mount helper defines a new network file system\\ntype, called `efs`, which is fully compatible with the standard `mount`\\ncommand in Linux. The mount helper also supports mounting an EFS file system at\\ninstance boot time automatically by using entries in the `/etc/fstab`\\nconfiguration file on EC2 Linux instances.\\n\\n**Warning:**\\n\\nUse the `_netdev` option, used to identify network file systems, when\\nmounting your file system automatically. If `_netdev` is missing, your EC2\\ninstance might stop responding. This result is because network file systems need to be\\ninitialized after the compute instance starts its networking. For more information, see\\nAutomatic mounting fails and the instance is unresponsive.\\n\\nYou can mount a file system by specifying one of the following properties:\\n\\n* **File system DNS name** \u2013 If you use the file system DNS name,\\n and the mount helper cannot resolve it, for example when you are mounting\\n a file system in a different VPC, it will fall back to using the mount target IP address. For more information, see\\n Mounting EFS file systems from another AWS account or VPC.\\n* **File system ID** \u2013 If you use the file system ID, the mount helper resolves it to the\\n local IP address of the mount target elastic network interface (ENI) without calling external resources.\\n* **Mount target IP address** \u2013 You can use the IP address of one of the file systems mount targets.\\n\\nYou can find the value for all of these properties in the Amazon EFS console. The file system\\nDNS name is found in the **Attach** screen.\\n\\nWhen encryption of data in transit is declared as a mount option for your EFS\\nfile system, the mount helper initializes a client `stunnel` process, and a\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/efs-mount-helper.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Mounting on EC2 Linux instances using the EFS mount helper\",\"context\":\"# Mounting on EC2 Linux instances using the EFS mount helper\\n\\nThis procedure requires the following:\\n\\n* You have installed the `amazon-efs-utils` package on the Amazon EC2\\n instance. For more information, see Manually installing the Amazon EFS client.\\n* You have created mount targets for the file system. For more information, see Managing mount targets.\\n\\n###### To mount your EFS file system using the mount helper on EC2 Linux instances\\n\\n1. Open a terminal window on your EC2 instance through Secure Shell (SSH), and\\n log in with the appropriate user name. For more information, see\\n Connect to your\\n EC2 instance in the\\n *Amazon EC2 User Guide*.\\n2. Create a directory `efs` that you will use as the file system mount point using the following command:\\n\\n ```\\n sudo mkdir efs\\n ```\\n3. Run one of the following commands to mount your file system.\\n\\n **Note:**\\n\\n If the EC2 instance and the file system you are mounting are located in different\\n AWS Regions, see Mounting EFS file systems from a different AWS Region to edit the `region` property in\\n the `efs-utils.conf` file.\\n\\n * To mount using the file system id:\\n\\n ```\\n sudo mount -t efs file-system-id efs-mount-point/\\n ```\\n\\n Use the ID of the file system you are mounting in place `file-system-id` and `efs` in place of `efs-mount-point`.\\n\\n ```\\n sudo mount -t efs fs-abcd123456789ef0 efs/\\n ```\\n\\n Alternatively, if you want to use encryption of data in transit, you can mount your\\n file system with the following command.\\n\\n ```\\n sudo mount -t efs -o tls fs-abcd123456789ef0:/ efs/\\n ```\\n * To mount using the file system DNS name:\\n\\n ```\\n sudo mount -t efs -o tls file-system-dns-name efs-mount-point/\\n ```\\n\\n ```\\n sudo mount -t efs -o tls fs-abcd123456789ef0.efs.us-east-2.amazonaws.com efs/\\n ```\\n * To mount using the mount target IP address:\\n\\n ```\\n sudo mount -t efs -o tls,mounttargetip=mount-target-ip file-system-id efs-mount-point/\\n ```\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/mounting-fs-mount-helper-ec2-linux.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Prerequisites for using the EFS mount helper\",\"context\":\"# Prerequisites for using the EFS mount helper\\n\\nYou can mount an EFS file system on an Amazon EC2 instance using the Amazon EFS mount\\nhelper. To use the mount helper, you need the following:\\n\\n* **File system ID of the file system to mount** - The\\n EFS mount helper resolves the file system ID to the local IP address of the\\n mount target elastic network interface (ENI) without calling external resources.\\n* **An EFS mount target**\\n \u2013 You create mount targets in your virtual private cloud (VPC). If you create your\\n file system in the console using the service recommended settings, a mount target is\\n created in each Availability Zone in the AWS Region that the file system is in. For\\n instructions to create mount targets, see Managing mount targets.\\n\\n **Note:**\\n\\n We recommend that you wait 60 seconds after the newly created mount target's\\n lifecycle state is **available** before mounting the file system via\\n DNS. This wait lets the DNS records propagate fully in the AWS Region where the file\\n system resides.\\n\\n If you use a mount target in an Availability Zone different from that of your EC2\\n instance, you incur standard EC2 charges for data sent across Availability Zones. You\\n also might see increased latencies for file system operations.\\n* For mounting One Zone file systems from a\\n different Availability Zone:\\n\\n + **The name of the file system's Availability Zone** \u2013 If you are\\n mounting an EFS One Zone file system that is located in a\\n different Availability Zone than the EC2 instance.\\n + **Mount target DNS name** \u2013 Alternatively, you can specify\\n the mount target's DNS name instead of the Availability Zone.\\n* **An EC2 instance running one of the supported Linux or\\n macOS distributions** \u2013 The supported distributions for mounting your\\n file system with the mount helper are the following:\\n\\n + Amazon Linux 2\\n + Amazon Linux 2023\\n + Amazon Linux 2017.09 and newer\\n + macOS Big Sur\\n + Red Hat Enterprise Linux (and derivatives such as CentOS) version 7 and\\n newer\\n + Ubuntu 16.04 LTS and newer\\n\\n **Note:**\\n\\n EC2 Mac instances running macOS Big Sur support NFS 4.0 only.\\n* **The EFS mount helper is installed on the EC2\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/mount-helper-prerequisites.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Check current AWS docs on mounting EFS on EC2"}

{"id": "0b04b5ca-2b75-4a0b-8489-7a3344bed5f5", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Here's the standard way to mount an EFS file system on an EC2 instance using the **EFS mount helper** (the recommended method for Linux/macOS instances):

### Prerequisites
- An EC2 instance running a supported OS (Amazon Linux 2/2023, RHEL/CentOS 7+, Ubuntu 16.04+, or macOS Big Sur)
- A mount target created for the file system in your VPC (created automatically if you used the console's recommended settings)
- The security group on the mount target allows NFS traffic (port 2049) from the EC2 instance

### Steps

1. **Install the mount helper** (`amazon-efs-utils`) on the instance, e.g. on Amazon Linux:
   ```
   sudo yum install -y amazon-efs-utils
   ```

2. **SSH into the instance** and create a mount point directory:
   ```
   sudo mkdir efs
   ```

3. **Mount the file system** — pick one of these:
   - By file system ID:
     ```
     sudo mount -t efs fs-abcd123456789ef0:/ efs/
     ```
   - By file system ID with encryption in transit:
     ```
     sudo mount -t efs -o tls fs-abcd123456789ef0:/ efs/
     ```
   - By DNS name:
     ```
     sudo mount -t efs -o tls fs-abcd123456789ef0.efs.us-east-2.amazonaws.com efs/
     ```

4. **(Optional) Auto-mount at boot** — add an entry to `/etc/fstab` using the `_netdev` option, which is important: without it, the instance can hang on boot since the network filesystem needs networking initialized first.

A few notes:
- EFS doesn't support mounting from EC2 **Windows** instances — Linux/macOS only.
- If the EC2 instance and file system are in different Availability Zones, you'll incur cross-AZ data charges and may see higher latency.
- If mounting right after creating a mount target, wait ~60 seconds for DNS to propagate before mounting by DNS name.
